n: Approach to Fever in Adults and Children

faq.a: If the patient has fever, recent travel to a malaria‑endemic area, and no obvious focus, start empiric artesunate while arranging a test.
faq.q: When should I start antimalarial treatment without a test?

faq.a: If the child is well‑appearing and fever <39 °C for <24 h, observe; obtain cultures if fever persists >48 h or red flags appear.
faq.q: How long should I observe a child with fever before ordering cultures?

exam: What immediate investigations would you order for a febrile patient with a recent malaria travel history and why — answer should include malaria RDT, full blood count, and urine dipstick, explaining each test’s purpose.

A 30‑year‑old HIV‑positive man presents with fever and cough; how do you differentiate TB from bacterial pneumonia and which test is most decisive — discuss sputum microscopy/GeneXpert versus chest X‑ray.
Explain why paracetamol is preferred over ibuprofen in a patient with suspected severe malaria — focus on renal safety and bleeding risk.
A child with sickle‑cell disease has fever 38.5 °C; list the top three causes you must rule out and the rapid steps to manage each — include sepsis, osteomyelitis, and vaso‑occlusive crisis.

Describe the clinical signs that would make you suspect meningitis in a febrile adult and the urgent management steps — highlight neck stiffness, photophobia, and immediate ceftriaxone plus dexamethasone.
How would you modify your work‑up if a basic laboratory cannot perform blood cultures? — suggest empirical broad‑spectrum antibiotics and reliance on clinical scoring.
Identify two red‑flag features that mandate referral to a higher‑level facility and justify their urgency — altered mental status and hemodynamic instability.
Why might a normal white‑cell count be misleading in severe malaria, and what alternative marker would you monitor — explain parasite density and lactate levels.
ai.title: Approach to Fever in Adults and Children
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: A systematic method to evaluate fever, focusing on history, examination, likely tropical causes, and pragmatic investigations for low‑resource settings. Emphasises red flags, common differentials, and step‑wise management without relying on unavailable tests.

b: Measure temperature with a reliable device; repeat if uncertain.
Document time, method, and associated symptoms.
sections.p: Fever is a regulated rise in core temperature ≥38.0 °C measured orally or rectally, reflecting a change in the hypothalamic set‑point.

b: Mild: 38.0–38.9 °C, well‑appearing.
Moderate: 39.0–40.0 °C, tachycardia, dehydration risk.
Severe: >40.0 °C or any temperature with altered mental status, hypotension, or organ failure.
sections.p: Severity is judged by temperature, systemic response, and organ dysfunction. Staging guides urgency of investigation.

b: Infections: malaria, bacterial sepsis, tuberculosis, HIV‑related opportunistic infections, typhoid, urinary‑tract infection, pneumonia.
Inflammatory/autoimmune: rheumatic fever, systemic lupus, sickle‑cell vaso‑occlusive crisis.
Other: drug fever, heat stroke, malignancy, post‑operative fever.
sections.p: Classify by infection, inflammation, and other systemic triggers, prioritising conditions common in East Africa and low‑resource hospitals.

b: History: duration, pattern, travel, exposure to malaria, HIV status, immunizations, recent antibiotics.
Exam: look for meningismus, lung crackles, abdominal tenderness, joint swelling, rash, hepatosplenomegaly.
sections.p: Fever may be isolated or accompanied by constitutional symptoms, organ‑specific signs, or a clear focus of infection.
Select tests that answer a specific clinical question; adapt when resources are limited.

t.b: Is there leukocytosis, anemia, or thrombocytopenia? Guides infection vs. marrow suppression.

t.a: Malaria rapid diagnostic test (RDT) or thick smear
t.b: Is malaria present? Positive test confirms Plasmodium infection; if unavailable, treat empirically in high‑risk patients.
Is there bacteremia? Positive culture directs targeted antibiotics.
Is there a urinary‑tract infection? Positive leukocyte esterase/nitrites or organisms suggest UTI.
Is there pneumonia or TB? Infiltrate or cavitation supports pulmonary infection.
Is the patient immunocompromised? Positive result prompts opportunistic infection work‑up.
Is there an inflammatory response? Elevated values support infection but are non‑specific.

b: Altered mental status, seizures, or coma.
Persistent fever >48 h with hemodynamic instability.
Signs of meningitis (neck stiffness, photophobia).
Severe dehydration, hypotension, or organ failure.
sections.p: Identify patients who need urgent referral or intensive care.

b: Empiric antimalarial (artesunate‑based) if malaria likely and test unavailable.
Broad‑spectrum antibiotic (e.g., ceftriaxone) for suspected severe bacterial infection; avoid aminoglycosides if renal function unknown.
IV fluids 20 ml/kg for moderate dehydration; monitor urine output.
Treat HIV opportunistic infections according to local protocols; start cotrimoxazole prophylaxis if CD4 <200.
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause while providing supportive care; choose drugs that are safe, affordable, and available.

b: Repeat temperature and clinical status; adjust antibiotics based on culture results.
Educate on malaria prevention (bed nets, prophylaxis) and vaccination (typhoid, pneumococcus).
Screen household contacts for TB if pulmonary TB suspected.
sections.p: Re‑evaluate after 24–48 h; ensure source control and complete therapy.

b: Heat stroke – environmental exposure, no infectious source, requires rapid cooling.
Drug fever – temporal relation to new medication, resolves after withdrawal.
Hyperthyroidism – persistent low‑grade fever with weight loss, tachycardia.
sections.p: Conditions that mimic fever or cause temperature elevation.

b: Negative malaria RDT does not exclude low‑parasite density; consider repeat test or microscopy.
Normal white count may be seen in severe malaria or early sepsis.
Elevated CRP can occur in non‑infectious inflammation, leading to over‑use of antibiotics.
sections.p: Pitfalls in interpreting investigations in low‑resource settings.

whenToSeekHelp: Altered consciousness, seizures, or signs of meningitis
Hypotension, rapid pulse, or signs of shock
